terms.meaning: Heat passes from a hotter part of an object to a colder part, while the particles stay in their places.
Heat moves in liquids and gases because the heated particles themselves move.
Heat travels from a hot body without needing any material in between.
A material that does not let heat pass through it easily.
Rainwater seeping down through soil and rocks into the ground.
Water stored in the spaces between underground sediments and rocks.
An underground layer of sediments and rocks that holds water.

items.name: Pins on a heated strip
items.formula: Pins stuck with wax fall one by one, starting nearest the flame.
items.example: Heat reaches the nearest pin first and the farthest pin last.

items.name: Pots and handles
items.formula: Good conductors for the pot, poor conductors for the handle.
items.example: A steel pan with a wooden handle.

items.name: Air as an insulator
items.example: Two thin blankets together are warmer than one thick blanket, because of the air layer between them.

items.name: Walls that keep heat
items.formula: Hollow bricks, or double walls filled with mud and cow dung, keep houses comfortable.
items.example: Some Himalayan homes use double wooden walls filled this way.

items.name: Heated air
items.formula: Air expands, gets lighter and rises.
items.example: Smoke detectors go on the ceiling because smoke rises with hot air.

items.name: Heated water
items.formula: Warm water rises and cooler water sinks to take its place.
items.example: A grain of potassium permanganate shows a rising coloured streak.

items.name: Land and water
items.formula: Land heats up faster than water, and also cools down faster.
items.example: A bowl of soil warms up quicker in the Sun than a bowl of water.

items.name: Sea breeze (day)
items.formula: Warm air over land rises, and cooler air moves from sea to land.
items.example: Coastal houses have windows facing the sea.

items.name: Land breeze (night)
items.formula: Warm air over the sea rises, and cooler air moves from land to sea.
items.example: At night the land has cooled but the sea is still warm.

items.name: Colour of clothes
items.formula: Light colours reflect most of the heat. Dark colours absorb more.
items.example: White in summer, dark in winter.

items.name: All three together
items.formula: Conduction through the pan, convection in the water, radiation around the flame.
items.example: A pan of water on a fire uses all three. So does a Himalayan bukhari stove.

items.name: Stages of the water cycle
items.example: Water rises as vapour, forms clouds, and falls as rain, snow or hail.

items.name: Which soil lets water through fastest?
items.example: Gravel has wide open spaces, and clay has only tiny ones.

items.name: Why groundwater runs low
items.formula: Too much pumping, fewer plants, and concrete surfaces that stop water soaking in.
items.example: A paved city yard lets less rain into the ground.

items.name: Refilling groundwater
items.example: Ice stupas in Ladakh store winter water as ice, which melts slowly for irrigation.

mistakes.text: A breeze is named after where it comes from. A sea breeze blows from the sea towards the land.
In conduction the particles stay in place. In convection they move.
Radiation does not need air or any other material. The Sun’s heat reaches us through empty space.
